page: Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-480s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute instance featuring an AMD EPYC processor with 2 vCPUs mapped to 1 physical core via hyperthreading. The instance operates on the x86_64 architecture at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz, supported by 32 KB L1d cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 32 MB L3 cache. It includes 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding an 8.0 GB per core ratio, and is bundled with 480 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. CPU resources are allocated on a shared basis.

Benchmark results indicate polarized performance characteristics. Single-core CPU performance is strong, with stress-ng single-core testing placing in the top 10% and single-threaded compression and decompression tasks ranking in the top 25%. However, multi-core CPU performance drops to the middle 50%, and overall PassMark CPU scores fall into the bottom 25%. Memory bandwidth is mixed, with small-block cached reads performing in the bottom 25% while large-block uncached reads and writes remain average.

The shared CPU allocation introduces potential resource contention, which is reflected in weak database operations and low Redis SET throughput. Static web serving throughput is also low at 2.19 GB/sec. Consequently, this instance is best suited for memory-intensive but compute-light workloads, such as caching layers, small-scale development environments, or basic background processing tasks that benefit from the 16 GB RAM and 480 GB NVMe storage but do not require sustained, dedicated CPU performance.
description: Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-480s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute instance configured with 2 shared vCPUs on an AMD EPYC processor running at 2.0 GHz. It features 16.0 GB of RAM, 480 GB of local NVMe SSD storage, and a single public IPv4 address. While single-core CPU benchmarks show top-tier performance, multi-core metrics and overall PassMark scores fall into the average and weak categories, respectively. Memory bandwidth is mixed, with weak small-block cached reads but average large-block throughput. Due to its shared CPU allocation, the instance exhibits lower performance in database operations, Redis transactions, and static web serving. This hardware profile is best aligned with memory-heavy, non-compute-intensive workloads such as staging environments, caching, and lightweight data processing where high memory capacity and local NVMe storage are required but dedicated CPU cores are not.
